findings.quote: and likewise of the Epirotes, Acarnanians, and all the others to whom in a short time he became the cause of many benefits.
findings.problem: The Greek reads 'ἅμα δὲ τούτοις Ἠπειρωτῶν, Ἀκαρνάνων,... ὅσων ἑκάστοις ἀγαθῶν ἐν βραχεῖ χρόνῳ παραίτιος ἐγένετο': there is a gap after Ἀκαρνάνων, and the clause 'ὅσων ... ἀγαθῶν' is an indirect exclamation ('how many benefits to each'). The English invents 'and all the others' and reads on as if the sentence were whole; the lacuna is smoothed over.
findings.proposed_fix: and likewise of the Epirotes and Acarnanians [...] and of how many benefits he was in a short time the cause to each of them.

units.note: The preceding clause 'τὴν δὲ Πελοποννησίων καὶ Βοιωτῶν' has no verb in the Greek (probably also affected by the gap); the English supplies 'The same may be said'. Only the visible lacuna is flagged.
Final sentence breaks off at a seam; lacuna already marked [...] in English.

Numbers checked: fifteen (πεντεκαίδεκα), thirty (τριάκοντα), two thousand (δισχιλίους) all correct. In the last sentence the subject of διέδωκε is not expressed in the Greek (singular verb after plural subject); the English supplies 'the king'. Genuinely unstated, so no fix proposed.

findings.quote: Therefore the soldiers there stood speechless, amazed by the strangeness of the thing and at the same time, as they foresaw and feared what would happen, filled alike with dread and delight.
findings.problem: Greek: 'οἱ μὲν ἐκπεπληγμένοι τὸ παράδοξον, οἱ δὲ προορώμενοι καὶ δεδιότες τὸ συμβησόμενον, ἀχανεῖς ἅμα δὲ περιχαρεῖς ὄντες, ἕστασαν'. The οἱ μὲν ... οἱ δὲ contrast divides the men into two groups (some struck by the strangeness, others foreseeing and fearing the outcome); the English merges them into one group feeling both.
findings.proposed_fix: Therefore some stood struck by the strangeness of the thing, and others foresaw and feared what would happen, all of them alike speechless and overjoyed.

units.note: ἀχανεῖς ἅμα δὲ περιχαρεῖς is a slightly odd pairing; the fix keeps it as the Greek has it.
